sections.html:
New Hampshire sorts rentals into "restricted" and "nonrestricted" property, and the sorting decides whether a landlord needs a stated reason to end a tenancy. Under RSA 540:1-a, nonrestricted property includes a single-family house when the owner holds no more than three single-family houses at one time. It also includes a unit in an owner-occupied building with four or fewer dwelling units. Every other residential rental is restricted.

This matters when you plan to sell. A small landlord with one inherited house and a tenant is usually in the nonrestricted group. The owner of a five-unit building, or of four separate single-family rentals, is in the restricted group, and the tenant can be removed only for a reason the statute names.

  • Nonrestricted: the owner may end the tenancy with a written notice to quit and does not have to give a reason (RSA 540:2, I).
  • Restricted: the owner may end the tenancy only for a listed ground (RSA 540:2, II).
  • Either way, the notice has to follow RSA 540:3 and RSA 540:5, and the landlord has to go through the court to get possession.

Work out which group your property is in before you take an offer.

sections.h2: Grounds for ending a restricted tenancy
sections.html:
RSA 540:2, II lists the grounds, and a landlord cannot add to them. They are:

  • Nonpayment of rent that is due and in arrears, after a demand.
  • Substantial damage to the premises by the tenant, household members or guests.
  • Failure to comply with a material term of the lease.
  • Behavior that harms the health or safety of others, or refusing suitable temporary relocation during lead-paint abatement.
  • "Other good cause."
  • A lead exposure hazard that the owner will abate by a method that takes more than 30 days or removes the unit from the rental market.
  • Willful failure to prepare the unit for insect or rodent remediation after written notice.
  • A remaining cotenant who is the accused perpetrator of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking.
  • Lease expiration, for leases of 12 months or more, with at least 60 days of written non-renewal notice and a court filing within 6 months of expiration.

If you own restricted property with a tenant in place, a sale by itself is not a statutory reason to remove the tenant. Many owners in that spot sell the building with the tenancy intact, and a cash buyer who buys as-is can do that without waiting for a vacant unit.

For residential tenancies, 30 days' notice is enough in all cases, and 7 days applies for nonpayment, substantial damage and behavior that affects health or safety (RSA 540:3). The notice must give the reason with specificity, and a nonpayment notice must tell the tenant about any right to stop the eviction by paying what is owed.

SituationNotice or deadline
Residential tenancy, general30 days
Nonpayment, damage, health or safety behavior7 days
Lease expiration at restricted property60 days written non-renewal notice, filing within 6 months
Security deposit return30 days from end of tenancy
Deposit turned over to a new ownerAt transfer or within 5 days

A tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can stop it by paying all back rent plus $15, and this cure can be used three times in a 12-month period. The court's eviction process guide has the details.

sections.h2: What does the court process look like for a landlord who needs possession?
sections.html:
A landlord cannot remove a tenant without a court order, and the steps follow RSA 540:13. The sequence moves fast on paper, but one notice mistake can send the landlord back to the start.

  • The landlord serves a valid notice, waits for it to expire, then files a landlord and tenant writ with the court. A sheriff serves it on the tenant.
  • The writ is returnable 7 days after service, and the tenant must file an appearance by that date to contest.
  • If the tenant appears, the hearing is set within 10 days of filing, with notice mailed at least 6 days before.
  • If the tenant does not appear, the court mails a notice of default at least 3 days before it issues a writ of possession.
  • The landlord can claim unpaid rent, but money judgments in this case are capped at $1,500 per decision.
  • Either side can appeal: notice of intent within 7 days of the decision notice, then a Supreme Court appeal within 30 days.

At the hearing the landlord has to prove the reason by a preponderance of the evidence and show strict compliance with notice and service rules. A judge can grant a discretionary stay of up to 90 days, or the parties can agree to a pay-and-stay arrangement. Weigh that timeline when deciding whether to evict before selling or sell with the tenant in place. Free mediation is also offered before a case is filed, though a request does not stop the eviction clock.

A landlord can ask for no more than one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, and the deposit stays the tenant's money held in trust. RSA 540-A:6 sets the main rules.

  • The landlord gives a signed receipt that states the amount and where the deposit is held, unless the deposit was paid by check.
  • The landlord must also tell the tenant in writing to note existing repair needs within 5 days of occupancy.
  • A deposit held for one year or longer earns interest at the regular savings rate of the New Hampshire bank where it sits, and the tenant may ask for accrued interest every 3 years.
  • When the property is transferred, the landlord turns the deposit over to the new owner at closing or within 5 days, and tells the tenant by registered or certified mail who now holds it.

Once the landlord hands over the deposit with interest, the landlord is relieved of liability and the new owner is responsible for returning it. Put that transfer on your closing checklist, along with a list of every deposit and its amount.

The return deadline is 30 days from the end of the tenancy under RSA 540-A:7. Deductions need a written, itemized list with evidence of the repair, and wear and tear cannot be charged. A landlord who breaches RSA 540-A:6, IV or 540-A:7 can owe twice the deposit plus interest under RSA 540-A:8. Deposits unclaimed for 6 months after the tenancy ends become the landlord's, absent fraud.

sections.h2: What can a landlord never do to a tenant?
sections.html:
No self-help to force a tenant out. RSA 540-A:3 bars the following:

  • Shutting off water, heat, electricity or gas, even when the landlord does not control the service, except for brief interruptions during actual repairs or emergencies.
  • Locking the tenant out or otherwise denying access except through proper judicial process.
  • Entering the unit without consent, except for emergency repairs or under a court order.

After a tenant moves out, the landlord must use reasonable care in storing belongings for 7 days, and the tenant can retrieve them without paying rent or storage fees.

Retaliation is also a defense. Under RSA 540:13-a, a tenant can defend against an eviction brought in retaliation for reporting a suspected RSA 540-A violation or a substantial housing code problem in good faith, for using the statute, or for meeting with other tenants. The defense does not apply if the tenant owes a week's rent or more.

sections.h2: Selling a rental that still has tenants
sections.html:
You can sell a rental with the tenant in place, as long as the deposit transfer and notice rules are followed. The sale does not cancel the tenant's rights, and a pending sale is not a listed ground for ending a restricted tenancy.

  • Pull the lease, the deposit records and any written notices before you talk to buyers.
  • Decide whether the property is restricted or nonrestricted, since that controls your options.
  • If you want the unit empty, use a lawful notice for a listed ground, or negotiate a move-out through mediation.
  • If you sell occupied, plan the deposit handoff and the certified-mail notice to each tenant.

An as-is cash buyer can often close without the unit being vacant or repaired, which is why owners with a difficult tenancy ask us about it. For questions about a specific notice, call the court's Information Center at 1-855-212-1234 or consult a New Hampshire attorney.

faqs.q: How much notice does a New Hampshire landlord have to give to end a residential tenancy?
faqs.a: Thirty days in most cases, and 7 days for nonpayment of rent, substantial damage, or behavior that affects health or safety. The notice has to give the reason with specificity, under RSA 540:3.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict a tenant just because the house is being sold?
faqs.a: At nonrestricted property, such as a single-family house when the owner holds no more than three, the owner can end the tenancy with a written notice to quit without giving a reason.

faqs.q: What happens to the security deposit when a New Hampshire rental is sold?
faqs.a: The seller turns the deposit over to the new owner at transfer or within 5 days and notifies the tenant by registered or certified mail. The new owner then becomes responsible for returning it.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: Thirty days from the end of the tenancy. A landlord who fails to comply can owe the tenant twice the deposit plus interest under RSA 540-A:8.

faqs.q: Is there free mediation for New Hampshire landlords and tenants?
faqs.a: Yes. The Office of Mediation and Arbitration offers free mediation before an eviction case is filed. A request does not stop the eviction process, so act quickly if a notice has been served.
